title: PQC & Digital Assets: Part 5 - Custody & Wallets: Institutional Custody & Exchanges
description: The institutions holding other people's bitcoin cannot wait for the protocol debates in Part 3 to resolve. Their clients, insurers and regulators are starting to ask for dated post-quantum plans now. This part covers what the custodians have actually done, which is less than the press releases suggest and more than nothing.

title: PQC & Digital Assets: Part 4 - Ethereum & L2s: Protocol Quantum Roadmap
description: Ethereum is the only major chain with a staffed team, a published roadmap and running test networks devoted to post-quantum migration. The work began in earnest in January 2026 and Vitalik Buterin has publicly confirmed the timeline. The strategy differs from Bitcoin's proposals in Part 3 in a basic way. Instead of a deadline that sunsets old signatures, Ethereum plans to let each account switch to new cryptography on its own schedule.

title: PQC & Digital Assets: Part 3 - Bitcoin: Protocol Proposals & Activation Politics
description: Bitcoin has no quantum-resistant way to hold coins today, and no activation scheduled to create one. What it has is a set of draft proposals at different levels of ambition. Add to that a live demonstration of how hard activating anything has become, and one workaround that needs no permission at all.

title: PQC & Digital Assets: Part 2 - Bitcoin: Exposure & Migration Analytics
description: Somewhere between 1.6 million and 7 million bitcoin are exposed to a future quantum attacker, depending on who is counting and what they count. That spread is the central finding of this part, and it is a definitional dispute rather than a measurement one. The analytics firms broadly agree on the underlying blockchain data. They disagree about whether coins that owners could protect today belong in the same total as coins that cannot be protected at all. No headline exposure figure from this subject means anything without its definition attached.

title: PQC & Digital Assets: Part 1 - Asset-Specific Threat Signals: ECC Attack Demonstrations & Resource Estimates
description: Nobody has broken a real cryptographic key with a quantum computer. Everything in this part sits against that fact. What exists instead is a contested prize demonstration and two rival estimates of the hardware a real attack would need. Alongside them sits a piece of arithmetic about how fast such an attack would have to run.

title: PQC & Digital Assets: Reading Guide
description: Digital Asset Cryptography is a survey of a threat that has not arrived and of an industry deciding what to do about it anyway. No quantum computer capable of breaking a deployed cryptographic key exists. Several million bitcoin would be exposed if one did. Between those two facts sits everything in this collection: contested demonstrations, rival hardware estimates, draft protocol changes, custody products and the beginnings of regulatory pressure.

title: CAB-Forum Watch: Part 5 - Revocation & Transparency
description: Revocation and transparency are the two mechanisms that let the web recover from a certificate that should not exist. Revocation withdraws trust from a certificate already issued. Transparency makes every issued certificate publicly visible, so that a bad one can be found at all. Section 1 covers revocation, where the industry's answer has shifted from fixing the mechanism to routing around it. Section 2 covers Certificate Transparency, which is undergoing its first architectural change since it was standardized.

title: CAB-Forum Watch: Part 4 - Public Trust Programs
description: The Forum writes the rules, and the root programs decide who is trusted. That division matters because a root program can and does impose requirements the Baseline Requirements do not, often a year or more ahead of them. This part covers both halves of that enforcement layer. Section 1 covers the four browser and operating system root store policies. Section 2 covers the Common CA Database and the incident and distrust record that runs through it.

title: CAB-Forum Watch: Part 3 - S/MIME Working Group
description: The S/MIME Working Group writes the rules for certificates that sign and encrypt email. Its Baseline Requirements are the youngest of the Forum's documents, adopted at the start of 2023, and the group has issued fifteen revisions since. Section 1 covers the current requirements and the version history behind them. Section 2 covers the RSA key size transition, whose first deadline falls two weeks after this report.

title: CAB-Forum Watch: Part 2 - Code Signing Working Group
description: The Code Signing Working Group writes the rules for the certificates that sign software. It is a smaller and slower group than the one governing web server certificates, and its recent record contains a useful lesson about reading a standards body correctly. Section 1 covers the published requirements and the ballots that produced them. Section 2 covers the work now in progress.

title: CAB-Forum Watch: Part 1 - Server Certificate Working Group
description: The Server Certificate Working Group writes the rules for the certificates that secure the public web. It is the busiest of the Forum's groups, and it published seven versions of its Baseline Requirements between November 2025 and August 2026.

title: CAB-Forum Watch: Reading Guide
description: The CA/Browser Forum decides what a publicly trusted certificate may contain, how its holder must be checked, and how long it may live. Its decisions reach almost every encrypted connection on the internet, and they are made in public by a body most people have never heard of. This collection follows that body and the browser root programs that enforce its rules.

title: Quantum Computing: Part 10 - Industry, Academia & Claims: Applications & Benchmarking Claims
description: This part records claims that quantum computers have done something useful, together with the rebuttals those claims attracted. The two belong in the same document. A quantum advantage claim and its classical refutation are usually separated by months and reported by different outlets, and reading either alone gives a false picture.

title: Quantum Computing: Part 9 - Industry, Academia & Claims: Academic & Theoretical
description: This part covers theory rather than machines. It records new algorithms and proofs about what quantum computers can and cannot do faster than classical ones. It also records the steady work of showing that some claimed quantum advantages were never real.

title: Quantum Computing: Part 8 - Industry, Academia & Claims: SPAC Mergers & Public Listings
description: Between February and August 2026, six quantum computing companies became publicly traded. Five did it by merging with a special purpose acquisition company, usually shortened to SPAC. A SPAC is a listed shell company holding cash and looking for a business to combine with. The sixth ran a conventional initial public offering.

title: Quantum Computing: Part 7 - Industry, Academia & Claims: Industry & Funding Moves
description: This part covers the money and the organizations rather than the science. It records who is paying for quantum computing, what governments have committed, which machines national laboratories have actually bought, and what companies have promised to deliver and by when.

title: Quantum Computing: Part 6 - Error Correction & Logical Qubits
description: A quantum computer's parts are unreliable in a way ordinary computer parts are not. Error correction is the engineering answer, and it works by spreading one unit of protected information across many unreliable physical ones. The protected unit is called a logical qubit, and the number of physical qubits it costs is the field's central price.

title: Quantum Computing: Part 5 - Hardware by Modality: Spin Qubits
description: A spin qubit stores information in the magnetic orientation of a single electron, held inside a silicon structure called a quantum dot. The qubits are roughly a hundred nanometres across, which makes them thousands of times smaller than the superconducting circuits in Part 1.

title: Quantum Computing: Part 4 - Hardware by Modality: Photonic Quantum Computing
description: Photonic quantum computers use particles of light as their qubits. Light does not need to be cooled, and does not pick up noise from its surroundings the way matter does. It travels through ordinary optical fibre, so a photonic machine can be spread across several racks or even several rooms. Most of the systems in this part run at room temperature apart from their detectors.

title: Quantum Computing: Part 3 - Hardware by Modality: Neutral Atom Qubits
description: Neutral atom machines hold uncharged atoms in place with focused laser beams called optical tweezers, and make them interact by exciting them into large, puffed-up states known as Rydberg states. The atoms are identical by nature, like the ions in Part 2. They are not electrically charged, so they can be packed far more densely without pushing each other apart.

title: Quantum Computing: Part 2 - Hardware by Modality: Trapped Ion Qubits
description: A trapped-ion quantum computer uses individual charged atoms, held in place by electric fields inside a vacuum chamber, as its qubits. Every ion of a given element is identical, which removes the manufacturing variation that troubles the chips in Part 1. Ions also hold their state far longer, and any ion in a chain can interact with any other rather than only its neighbours.

title: Quantum Computing: Part 1 - Hardware by Modality: Superconducting Qubits
description: Superconducting qubits are tiny circuits, cooled to near absolute zero, that behave like artificial atoms. They are the most widely deployed way to build a quantum computer, and the approach behind most of the machines the public has heard of. They are fast, they are manufacturable using methods borrowed from the chip industry, and they lose their information quickly. Everything in this part follows from that last trade.

title: Quantum Computing: Reading Guide
description: Quantum Computing is a survey of an industry at an awkward moment. The central scientific question of the last decade has been answered. The machines still cannot do anything commercially useful. Billions of dollars of public and private money moved into the field during 2026 anyway. This collection covers all three of those facts and the tension between them.

title: PQC Mathematics: Part 5 - Primitives & Cryptanalysis: Cryptanalysis of Candidate & Non-Ratified Schemes
description: This part covers attacks on algorithms that are not yet standards. That distinction matters, because an attack on a candidate is how the process is supposed to work. A scheme that fails during evaluation has done its job by failing early.

title: PQC Mathematics: Part 4 - Primitives & Cryptanalysis: Symmetric & Hash-Based Research
description: The usual summary of quantum computing's effect on cryptography is that public-key algorithms break and symmetric ones merely need longer keys. That summary is right about AES and wrong about almost everything built on top of it.

title: PQC Mathematics: Part 3 - Standards Tracks & Candidates: Candidate Asymmetric Algorithms
description: This part covers the algorithms NIST did not choose. Some lost a competition. Some were never entered. Two have been standardized anyway, by other bodies, which is why they matter more than the word "candidate" suggests.

title: PQC Mathematics: Part 2 - Standards Tracks & Candidates: Non-NIST National & Regional Standards Tracks
description: NIST is not the only body choosing post-quantum algorithms. South Korea ran its own competition and picked its own winners. China is running a second one and has said openly that it intends to shape international norms rather than adopt American standards. Germany and France endorse algorithms NIST did not select, and require them in combination rather than alone.

title: PQC Mathematics: Part 1 - Standards Tracks & Candidates: NIST Standards Track
description: NIST runs the process that decides which post-quantum algorithms the world will actually use. Its choices are not binding on anyone outside the US federal government, but in practice they set the direction for browsers, cloud providers, hardware vendors and most other standards bodies.

title: PQC Mathematics: Reading Guide
description: Post-Quantum Mathematics covers the layer underneath the migration. A companion collection, Post-Quantum Cryptography Migration, covers the deployment of the new algorithms across real systems. This one covers where those algorithms come from, who is choosing them, what the alternatives are, and what is being broken.

title: PQC Migration: Part 19 - Finding & Governing It: Governance, Mandates & Timelines
description: Every earlier part of this collection describes technology. This one describes the deadlines. Governments have converted post-quantum guidance into dates with consequences, and the dates now drive vendor roadmaps more than the physics does.

title: PQC Migration: Part 18 - Finding & Governing It: Developer & Migration Tooling
description: Before an organization can migrate anything, it has to find its cryptography, and almost none can. Asking which systems use RSA is a question most enterprises cannot answer in minutes, or at all. The tools that fix that, inventories, scanners, validators, and test rigs, are this report's subject.

title: PQC Migration: Part 17 - Edges & Sectors: Financial Messaging & Sector Rails
description: The world's money moves through a small set of rails: SWIFT messages between banks, central-bank settlement systems, and the card networks. Their cryptography is old, their message formats are tight, and a successful quantum attack on any of them would be a macroeconomic event. One study put a theoretical attack on the U.S. settlement system at a 10 to 17 percent hit to GDP.

title: PQC Migration: Part 16 - Edges & Sectors: Enterprise IoT & OT
description: The physical world runs on devices that live for decades: grid controllers, payment cards, cars, satellites, smart meters. They are the hardest things to migrate and the last to move, which makes this report a map of gaps as much as progress.

title: PQC Migration: Part 15 - Where It Runs: Email & Messaging
description: Messages are the purest harvest-now-decrypt-later target: personal, durable, and often archived by the recipient for years. That has made the secure messengers the most advanced post-quantum deployments anywhere, while email, the older medium, mostly waits on the layers beneath it.

title: PQC Migration: Part 14 - Where It Runs: Enterprise Applications & Delivery
description: The applications businesses actually live in, the ERP system, the video call, the remote desktop, are the last stop of the migration. Everything beneath them has to work first, and their vendors mostly move by inheriting the layers below.

title: PQC Migration: Part 13 - Where It Runs: Enterprise Infrastructure & Storage
description: The machines that run and store enterprise data live longer than almost anything else in computing. A storage array, a tape cartridge, or a server management chip bought today will still be in service when quantum computers are far closer. That makes this hardware's cryptography a decision with a decade-long tail.

title: PQC Migration: Part 12 - Where It Runs: Security & Network Appliances
description: The boxes that guard networks, firewalls, load balancers, routers, and encryptors, have become one of the migration's busiest fronts. Every major vendor now ships or roadmaps post-quantum features, and some sell hardware designed around the new algorithms from the silicon up.

title: PQC Migration: Part 11 - Where It Runs: Cloud Infrastructure
description: Most of the world's computing now runs in a handful of clouds, so a single provider decision moves more traffic to post-quantum than a thousand enterprise projects. The providers know it, and they have turned the migration into a competitive race with published roadmaps and dated milestones.

title: PQC Migration: Part 10 - Building & Shipping Software: Containers, Orchestration, Service Mesh
description: Cloud-native infrastructure got much of its post-quantum protection by accident. Kubernetes, containerd, and their neighbors are written in Go, and when Go turned hybrid key exchange on by default, whole clusters started negotiating it with no announcement and no planning.

title: PQC Migration: Part 9 - Building & Shipping Software: Software Supply Chain
description: Every piece of software you install was vouched for by a signature: the package manager checked it, the app store checked it, the container runtime checked it. Those signatures are almost all classical, and unlike a TLS session they must stay valid for years. Forging one retroactively would poison the supply chain at its source.

title: PQC Migration: Part 8 - Building & Shipping Software: Application Dev Stacks & Languages
description: The software that developers actually build with, web servers, language runtimes, database drivers, and browsers, mostly does not implement cryptography. It inherits it. When OpenSSL, Go, or the operating system's TLS stack turns post-quantum on, thousands of products above them change behavior at once.

title: PQC Migration: Part 7 - Protocols & Trust: PKI, Certificates, Identity & Authentication
description: Everything that proves identity on the internet runs on certificates and signatures, and none of it is quantum-safe yet. Encryption moved first because recorded traffic is at risk today. Signatures can wait until a large quantum computer exists, but the systems that issue, distribute, and validate them take a decade to change. This is the migration's long pole.

title: PQC Migration: Part 6 - Protocols & Trust: Network & Transport Protocols
description: The protocols that move data across networks are where post-quantum cryptography first became real. Every encrypted connection made today can be recorded and decrypted later by a quantum computer, so key exchange had to move first, years ahead of signatures.

title: PQC Migration: Part 5 - Cryptographic Foundations: HSMs, KMS & Key Management
description: Hardware security modules, key managers, and the standards around them are where organizations keep their most sensitive cryptographic keys. This layer has to adopt post-quantum algorithms before much else can. A certificate authority or a payments network can only move to a new algorithm once the hardware beneath it supports that algorithm and auditors accept the result.

title: PQC Migration: Part 4 - Cryptographic Foundations: Crypto Libraries & Providers
description: Almost no application implements cryptography itself. It calls a library. A few dozen libraries therefore decide when the world's software actually becomes quantum-resistant, whatever the standards say.

title: PQC Migration: Part 3 - Operating Systems: Operating Systems & Endpoints
description: Operating systems are where post-quantum cryptography meets ordinary users. When an OS ships the new algorithms, every application on it can use them. When it turns them on by default, every user gets them without knowing.

title: PQC Migration: Part 2 - Silicon & Firmware: Firmware & Root of Trust
description: Every computer decides what software to trust before the operating system even starts. That decision rests on cryptographic signatures burned into firmware, boot chains, and security chips. These are the hardest components to fix after they ship, so they carry the earliest post-quantum deadlines in the whole migration.

title: PQC Migration: Part 1 - Silicon & Firmware: Hardware Acceleration & Silicon
description: The new post-quantum algorithms are only useful if hardware can run them fast. This report covers that problem in three sections. Section 1 follows the tuned code that makes the new math fast on ordinary processors. Section 2 follows the dedicated accelerator cards built for heavy connection loads. Section 3 follows the ready-made circuit blocks that put the algorithms into future chips.

title: PQC Migration: Reading Guide
description: Post-Quantum Cryptography Migration is a survey of one large, slow-moving event: the replacement of the public-key cryptography that secures nearly all digital communication. Quantum computers, once large enough, will break the algorithms in use today. Standards bodies have chosen replacements, and deploying them now touches every layer of computing, from silicon to government policy.
